title: Al-Qadir, the Able
tomorrow: what does a crunchy dry leaf have to do with God's power?

lines: THE FRIEND WHO SHOOTS THEIR SHOT.
cards: Every group chat has the friend who shoots their shot: the reach school, the audition, the long-shot text. And the friend who says, don't embarrass yourself.
Yesterday's question: asking God for the impossible, bold or rude? Inside Islam, serious people have leaned both ways, from real texts. Today's Name sits right in the middle of the argument.

teach.h: ALLAH IS ABLE TO DO ALL THINGS.
teach.b: Al-Qadir, the Able. Pickthall's Qur'an keeps landing on a line built from it: "Lo! Allah is Able to do all things." Side one says: then ask big.
The Qur'an tells of Zakariyya, an old man with a wife who could not have children, asking for a child anyway, and being answered.
And in Sahih Muslim the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people not to pray, forgive me if You wish.
Ask with resolve, he says, because nothing is too great for Allah to give.

teach.h: SIDE TWO: ASK HUMBLY, DON'T OVERSTEP.
teach.b: Side two doesn't tell you to stop asking. It reads another verse: "Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Lo! He loveth not aggressors."
Some scholars took that to include overstepping in du'a: asking for what God has already said won't happen, as if the request were a test He has to pass.
And a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad says no sincere du'a is wasted: it's granted, or a harm is turned away, or it's stored up for later.

So, on this view, ask, and let the answer take any of those shapes. Here's what the two share, and it's worth saying out loud: neither side says stay quiet. They argue about posture, not about whether to knock.
One knocks loudly. The other knocks humbly.
Both are knocking on the door of the Able.

how: Muslims make du'a in their own words at any time, often with raised hands, and may call on Allah by a Name that fits the request, as in ya Qadir.

o: the Judge, who weighs every request made
the Patient, who waits a long time to act
the Able, with power to do all things

games.q: who says what in the debate — tap the pairs.
p: asked for a child in old age

s: the Prophet taught people to add 'if You wish' to their du'a
he taught the opposite: ask with resolve, for nothing is too great for Allah to give.
Zakariyya asked for a child when it seemed too late
the Qur'an tells it: an old man, a wife who couldn't have children, and he asked anyway.
a du'a that isn't granted is simply wasted
a hadith says a sincere du'a is granted, or turns away a harm, or is stored up.

games.q: class debate: you argue 'ask God boldly for anything.' your partner gets the other side, from inside Islam. what's their strongest case?
o: ask humbly: some read 7:55 as warning against asking for what God said won't be.
never ask for big things; du'a is only for forgiveness and small daily needs.
don't ask at all: everything is already written, so asking can't change a thing.
games.why: the real other side still asks. it draws its line around overstepping, asking for what God has said won't be, not around what merely looks unlikely.

practice: Name one thing that seems out of reach. Then name the real obstacle in one honest word, and one small step this week that's yours to take.
If you make du'a, ask for it with resolve, no if You wish; if not, hold the wish and the step side by side for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Qadir. The Able: the one with power to do all things, asked boldly by some and humbly by others, but asked.

orig.note: Arabic: the Able, who has power to do all things.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: able, whether you knock loudly or softly. Name sixty-nine, and the door is still open.

sources.q: Lo! Allah is Able to do all things.
Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Lo! He loveth not aggressors.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2679 (do not say 'forgive me if You wish'; ask with resolve, nothing is too great for Allah to give); also Sahih al-Bukhari 6339
Musnad Ahmad 11133 (a du'a is granted, or a harm averted, or stored up)
